Bayesian Meta Analysis on Lead Exposure & IQ Loss

Author

Paulina Sell

Published

July 25, 2025

Introduction

The aim of this project is to estimate the Environmental Burden of Disease (EBD) attributable to lead exposure in Germany. Here, we will focus on the neurodevelopmental effects of lead, therefore the health outcome will be IQ point loss in children and adolescents. In order to estimate these population health effects, we need to find solid evidence for exactly how lead exposure is related to IQ loss. The exposure data we are working with is based on whole blood samples of 720 children and adolescents (ages 3 - 17) in Germany from the German Environmental Survey, GerES V. The data was collected between 2014 and 2017.

In order to quantify exactly how lead exposure is related to IQ loss, we turn to epidemiological literature. There are many studies published focusing on the the neurodevelopmental effects of lead. Instead of just choosing one estimate from one study for our EBD analysis, we will pool estimates from multiple studies in order to gather and strengthen the evidence we base our analysis on. And since uncertainty plays an important role in the final burden of disease results, we will use a Bayesian approach to meta analysis. With this approach we can easily model uncertainty and get a full posterior distribution of the pooled effect (instead of a mean effect and an hard-to-interpret confidence interval). Later, we will be able to use many draws from the posterior distribution for our EBD analysis! But first, let’s meta analyse some epi studies. I found this hands-on guide from Harrer et al. 2021 very helpful.

Step 1: Standardizing Effect Estimates

We first need to search for and identify relevant studies and extract the data necessary for our analysis. These tasks were already done by Philippe Palmont and his team at ANSES. Next, we need to harmonize / standardize the effect estimates before we can pool them. Most of the studies transformed their blood lead level (BLL) data to a logarithmic scale in order to fulfill the assumption of a linear relationship between BLL (exposure) and IQ points (outcome) for their regression analyses. Unfortunately, they did not always use the same log bases. Some used log10, some ln, and some log2. Also, 3 of the 14 included studies did not transform their BLL at all, so it’s on a linear scale. Philippe Palmont and his team standardized all estimates to linear increments of exposure in their analysis, using the template proposed by Rodriguez Barranco 2017. But what happens to the effect estimates, when we transform them in this way?

Visually Checking Transformations

Let’s compare the original beta coefficient from Crump et al. 2013 (ß = -2.65) for ln(BLL) with the transformed one (ß = ß -0.277), that now should be used for linear BLL.

This looks like we would likely underestimate the effect of lower BLL and overestimate the effect of higher BLL. Since today, BLL are often found to be much lower than even 30 µg/dL (in our sample, the range is ~0.04 to ~4.5 µg/dL), we would likely underestimate the population health effects of BLL on IQ in children. Transforming log estimates to linear seems to be problematic here.

Transforming Estimates to ln(BLL)

In order to preserve the correct exposure-response curves and harmonize the effect estimates for our meta analysis, we could try to transform all estimates to ln(BLL), since this closer to the original estimates reported by the studies, since they mostly just used different bases for their logarithmic transformations.

These are the formulas I used:
\[ \beta_{ln} = \beta_{linear} \times C_{ref}\ \] \[ \beta_{ln} = \frac{beta_{log_{2}}} {\ln(2)}\ \] \[ \beta_{ln} = \frac{beta_{log_{10}}} {\ln(10)}\ \] Where:
\(\beta_{ln}\) = harmonized beta coefficient (natural logarithm)
\(\beta_{linear}\) = original linear beta coefficient
\(\beta_{log_2}\) = original log₂-transformed beta coefficient
\(\beta_{log_{10}}\) = original log₁₀-transformed beta coefficient
\(C_{ref}\) = reference concentration for linear transformation

Case 1: log10(BLL) -> ln(BLL): Dantzer et al. 2020

We can’t even see the blue curve, so the transformation should be valid.

Case 2: log2(BLL) -> ln(BLL): Desrochers-Couture et al. 2018

For the transformation from log2 to ln, we can see that at least in this concentration range, the transformed estimate is a good approximation for the original one.
! Note that this study reported a small protective effect of lead exposure, this is why the curve is flipped.

Case 3: linear(BLL), not transformed -> ln(BLL): Iglesias et al. 2011

In order to transform this estimate, we need to set a reference BLL (\(C_{ref}\)). Here, I chose 2.2 µg/dL.

This looks problematic… The concentration range is quit high though, so let’s zoom in:

It looks like, even in the lower concentration range, the transformed estimate is not a good approximation of the original estimate. For my meta analysis, I therefore decided to exclude 3/14 studies with estimates for untransformed BLL data. We end up with 11 harmonized effect estimates for the association of ln(BLL) and absolute IQ point loss.

Step 2: Meta Analysis

Now that we have collected our study data and harmonized the effect estimates, we can finally begin our meta analysis!

Setting Priors

First, we need to set priors. We will be conservative and use weakly informative priors. For the main effect (\(μ\)), I chose \(μ \sim N(0, 1)\).

The prior for the heterogeneity (\(τ\)) is a bit more difficult to set since it must be, by definition, positive. Here, a half-Cauchy distribution can be useful. it is defined by two parameters: the location, which determines the center of the distribution, and the scale parameter, which controls the spread. Then, we set the lower limit to zero (lb = 0)) to make it half. For this model, I chose \(τ \sim HC(0, 0.5)\).

As you can see, we grant quite a high probability (20.48%) to the heterogeneity being higher than 1.5. This prior is relatively weakly informative if you consider the median of standard errors that we extracted from our included studies (1.29).

This is how we set our priors:

priors <- c(prior(normal(0,1), class = Intercept), 
            prior(cauchy(0,0.5), class = sd, lb = 0))

Fitting the model

Now we can write & fit the model, using the package brms by Bürkner 2017. In the second line, we specify our model. We set adapt_delta to 0.99 to decrease the step size that the sampling algorithm explores the posterior distribution with. If we don’t do this, adapt_delta will default to 0.8 and we get Warning: There were 5 divergent transitions after warmup. This means that the algorithm has trouble exploring the posterior distribution.

m.brm <- brm(
  beta_ln|se(se_beta_ln) ~ 1 + (1|author_year),
  data = data,
  prior = priors,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 4000,
  seed = 1223)

Assessing Convergence & Model Validity

Let’s first make sure that our priors are defined well enough. We can do this by doing a prior predictive check. Prior predictive checks are used to evaluate the suitability of prior distributions before the model “sees” our data. They involve simulating data from the model using only the prior distributions and then examining the simulated data to see if it aligns with our expectations. This can help to identify problems with the chosen priors, such as implausible parameter values, before they can influence the posterior distribution and final inferences. Here you can read more about prior & posterior predictive checks.

Now let’s do a posterior predictive check:

Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

Here, we should pay attention to the \(\hat{R}\) value (potential scale reduction factor), which tells us whether the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling process (this is the algorithm used to estimate the parameters) has converged. \(\hat{R}\) of less than 1.05 is generally considered good. Here you can read more about convergence and efficiency diagnostics for Markov Chains. As we can see, our \(\hat{R}\) values are both 1.00 which is good!

Now let’s look at the traceplots of the 4 MCMC chains for both the posterior distribution of beta (b_intercept) and the standard deviation of beta (as_author_year__Intercept). The red vertical lines indicate where the warm-up was finished (samples on from warm-up will not be used further).

# lets look at posterior distributions ----
# prepare data
post.samples <- as_draws_df(m.brm, variable = c("b_Intercept", "sd_author_year__Intercept"))

# generate density plot for posterior distributions
ggplot(aes(x = b_Intercept), data = post.samples) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightblue",                # set the color
               color = "lightblue", alpha = 0.7) +  
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(post.samples$b_Intercept), 
                               linetype = "dotted", 
                               color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Mode(post.samples$b_Intercept), 
             linetype = "dotted", 
             color = "blue") +
  labs(x = expression(italic(b_Intercept)),
       y = element_blank()) +
  theme_minimal()
#ggsave("results/posterior_dist_b_log_no-Halabicky-Iglesias-Min.png", width = 25, height = 15, units = "cm")


ggplot(aes(x = sd_author_year__Intercept), data = post.samples) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightgreen",               # set the color
               color = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.7) +  
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(post.samples$sd_author_year__Intercept), 
             linetype = "dotted", 
             color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Mode(post.samples$sd_author_year__Intercept), 
             linetype = "dotted", 
             color = "blue") +
  labs(x = expression(sd_author_year__Intercept),
       y = element_blank()) +
  theme_minimal()
# lets generate a forest plot ----
# first, we have to prepare the data and extract the posterior distribution for each individual study 
study.draws <- spread_draws(m.brm, r_author_year[author_year,], b_Intercept) %>% 
  mutate(b_Intercept = r_author_year + b_Intercept)

# Next: generate distribution of the pooled effect
pooled.effect.draws <- spread_draws(m.brm, b_Intercept) %>% 
  mutate(author_year = "Pooled Effect")

# Next: bind study.draws and pooled.effect.draws to one data frame. 
# We then start a pipe again, calling ungroup first, and then use mutate to clean the study labels (i.e. replace dots with spaces)
forest.data <- bind_rows(study.draws, 
                         pooled.effect.draws) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(author_year = str_replace_all(author_year, "[.]", " ")) %>%
  mutate(author_year = fct_rev(factor(author_year)))

# Lastly: forest plot should also display the effect size (SMD and credible interval) of each study. 
# We use forest.data data set, group it by Author, and then use the mean_qi function to calculate these values
forest.data.summary <- group_by(forest.data, author_year) %>% 
  mean_qi(b_Intercept)

# let's plot!
ggplot(aes(b_Intercept, 
           relevel(author_year, "Pooled Effect", # Y-axis uses author_year but reorders it so "Pooled Effect" appears at the bottom (after = Inf)
                   after = Inf)), 
       data = forest.data) +
  
  # Box to highlight pooled effect
  geom_rect(data = filter(forest.data.summary, author_year == "Pooled Effect"),
            aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, 
                ymin = as.numeric(factor(author_year)) - 0.4, 
                ymax = as.numeric(factor(author_year)) + 0.4),
            fill = "steelblue3", alpha = 0.2) +
  
  # Add vertical lines for pooled effect and CI
  geom_vline(xintercept = fixef(m.brm)[1, 1], # line at the pooled effect estimate
             color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.8, linetype = 2) + 
  #geom_vline(xintercept = fixef(m.brm)[1, 3:4], # lines for Q2.5 & Q97.5 from pooled effect (95 % CI)
             #color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.8, linetype = 2) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "gray20", 
             linewidth = 1) + # line at zero (null effect line)
  
  # Add density ridges
  geom_density_ridges(fill = "steelblue3", # ridge density plots for each study/row
                      rel_min_height = 0.01, # removes very small density values
                      col = NA, scale = 1, # no outline color, scale of distributions
                      alpha = 0.8) + # opacity
  
  # Add point estimates with confidence intervals
  geom_pointinterval(data = forest.data.summary,
                     aes(xmin = .lower, xmax = .upper),
                     fatten_point = 1.5,
                     linewidth = 0.8) +
  
  # Add text and labels
  geom_text(data = mutate_if(forest.data.summary,
                             is.numeric, round, 2), # decimals
            aes(label = glue("{b_Intercept} [{.lower}, {.upper}]"), # format text -> ß [CIlow, CIhigh]
                x = Inf), hjust = "inward") + #aligns text inward from the edge
  labs(x = "beta",
       y = element_blank()) +
  #xlim(-4, 1) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(panel.border = element_blank())
Picking joint bandwidth of 0.127
